1	---
2	name: evolution
3	description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, the record of what landed and how evolution itself evolves. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson."
4	---
5	
6	# Evolution
7	
8	How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
9	providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
10	campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
11	wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
12	evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
13	this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
14	[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.
15	
16	## 1. Goals
17	
18	Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
19	full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
20	are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.
21	
22	A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
23	its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
24	tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
25	analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
26	tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
27	extending what it does, proposed, not made.
28	<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->
29	
30	## 2. Signals
31	
32	Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:
33	
34	| signal | what it suggests |
35	|---|---|
36	| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
37	| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
38	| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
39	| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
40	| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
41	| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
42	| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
43	| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
44	| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
45	| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
46	| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |
47	
48	A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
49	finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
50	many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
51	something, is not made.
52	
53	## 3. Destinations
54	
55	Each signal goes to one destination:
56	
57	- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
58	  of Crustify;
59	- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
60	  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
61	- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
62	- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
63	- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
64	  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
65	  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.
66	
67	A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
68	blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
69	provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
70	agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
71	launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
72	the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
73	what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
74	assistant carries it out.
75	
76	The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
77	the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
78	would hold for any C codebase.
79	
80	## 4. Proposals
81	
82	A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as
83	its `PROPOSAL.md`: the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it
84	cites; its destination; the change, or the patch; how it was validated; its review's
85	verdict; and its status, `open`, `landed`, with the commit it landed as, or `declined`,
86	with why. A lesson is not
87	filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it.
88	
89	A defect in a tool found while reviewing is such a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed
90	code, and is filed with its reproducer.
91	
92	## 5. Lessons
93	
94	The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
95	before its first step. Each is one rule, with the evidence it rests on and its scope, the
96	modules, items or stages it holds for. A lesson a second campaign records again is
97	generalized into the spec, by a proposal citing both.
98	
99	## 6. Changes
100	
101	A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
102	that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
103	campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
104	needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
105	campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.
106	
107	A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
108	working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
109	made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
110	fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
111	[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
112	campaign's.
113	
114	- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
115	  as generally as the evidence allows.
116	- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
117	  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
118	  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
119	  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
120	  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
121	  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
122	- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
123	  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
124	  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
125	  merged upstream only with the user's approval.
126	
127	A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
128	landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.
129	
130	## 7. Validation
131	
132	A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.
133	
134	A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
135	the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
136	the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
137	after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
138	prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
139	effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.
140	
141	A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
142	watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [Record](#11-record) describes.
143	
144	## 8. Review
145	
146	Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
147	one that made it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks
148	that:
149	
150	- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;
151	- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;
152	- it is placed and written as [`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md) describes, and states
153	  no rule in the target's names;
154	- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
155	- its entry of [Record](#11-record), which the change or its proposal drafts, names a
156	  recurrence signal a campaign would observe, and `test` only where its test checks all of
157	  it; and
158	- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.
159	
160	A review runs under the campaign's working branch of the component, never under the change
161	it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
162	only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
163	verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. Its checks are this section's and its
164	role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
165	A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
166	tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
167	validation run again.
168	
169	The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
170	reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.
171	
172	What only records what was decided, a status of [Record](#11-record) a check changes or a
173	proposal's status, verdict and review, changes no rule and is not reviewed; an entry is
174	reviewed with its change.
175	
176	A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
177	detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
178	record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
179	each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.
180	
181	## 9. Autonomy
182	
183	The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:
184	
185	| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
186	|---|---|
187	| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
188	| `propose` | nothing but the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
189	| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
190	| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |
191	
192	A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it,
193	without the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else
194	runs on it. `GOALS.md` is the exception: a change to it is proposed, never made, since it
195	is what every other change is judged against.
196	
197	A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
198	the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
199	record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
200	first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
201	is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
202	they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
203	again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
204	soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
205	new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.
206	
207	A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
208	makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
209	reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
210	reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
211	batch is.
212	
213	## 10. Adoption
214	
215	Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
216	under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
217	describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
218	after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
219	revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
220	under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
221	defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
222	`revisit`.
223	
224	At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: recurring lessons are
225	proposed for the spec, open proposals are landed as the autonomy allows, the working
226	branches are offered to the user for `devel`, the revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled, and the watched changes
227	of the record are checked against the module, as an audit checks them at its end.
228	
229	## 11. Record
230	
231	Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
232	[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
233	campaign can tell whether it held. An entry gives the campaign and proposal the change
234	came from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence
235	signal and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change
236	no proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came
237	from. The entry is drafted with its change, in the change itself for a
238	change to Crustify and in its proposal for a change to a tool, so that the review reads it,
239	and is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign as the change lands. The record holds every
240	change landed since it began, on 2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.
241	
242	The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
243	campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
244	tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
245	it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
246	has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.
247	
248	A watched change is checked at each module's end, and at an audit's end, in every campaign,
249	against that module's or audit's findings, failed runs, proposals and corrections. It is:
250	
251	- `watched` from its landing;
252	- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
253	  cites the entry: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that
254	  passed it were; and
255	- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
256	  it, without the signal.
257	
258	The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign, each entry with its
259	change and each check at its module's end, and reaches `devel` with it. Rows are appended
260	in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge of two campaigns' working
261	branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
262	Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the check still runs and its statuses are
263	committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
264	with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, it does not run.
265	
266	## 12. Evolving evolution
267	
268	Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
269	campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
270	that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
271	met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
272	reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
273	its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
274	a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
275	from a fixed rule. Each is a
276	signal of this guidance, as [Signals](#2-signals) lists them, and its proposal is on this
277	skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.
278	
279	Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
280	what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
281	[Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.
282	---
283	name: versioning
284	description: "Repositories, branches, worktrees, landing under the landing lock, promotion, integration, their lifecycle, and the identity every commit takes. Read before the first commit, and before creating, landing on, promoting or purging any branch or worktree."
285	---
286	
287	# Versioning
288	
289	How a campaign's work is held in version control: the repositories it works in, their
290	branches and worktrees, how a batch lands its work and how each part is promoted. Where
291	things sit in the tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.
292	
293	## 1. Repositories
294	
295	A translation campaign produces a Rust codebase, so its repository is one: a new
296	repository created for the campaign, with the Rust at its root and the C it translates
297	inside it.
298	
299	| campaign | repository | the C, under `c/` |
300	|---|---|---|
301	| wrap | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the source, pinned at the campaign's revision, which the campaign never changes |
302	| port | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the campaign's fork of the source, `<repo>-fork`, on its `main` branch, which the modules' switches trim as they leave C |
303	
304	`<repo>` is the source repository's name: a campaign on libgit2 is `libgit2-crustify`,
305	and a port's fork `libgit2-fork`. A wrap and a port campaign share the name, since wrapping a
306	codebase is a step towards replacing its implementation: a port continues a wrap campaign
307	in its repository. Both keep the C's history where it belongs, so that it can be read in the
308	submodule and an upstream release taken in by rebasing the fork's `main` onto it. The fork
309	mirrors the source's own `main` as `upstream/main`. The repositories are created under the
310	`crustify-rs` organization; the campaign's tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.
311	
312	A library the target uses from outside its tree is wrapped in a wrap campaign of its own,
313	in `<source>-crustify`, named after the source it is built from, as
314	[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md) describes.
315	
316	An audit reviews an existing Rust crate in its own repository, and creates none.
317	
318	## 2. Branches
319	
320	| branch | name | checked out |
321	|---|---|---|
322	| shipping | `main` in the campaign's own repository; `crustify/main` in an audit, beside the reviewed crate's own branches | never while the campaign runs |
323	| working | `crustify/devel` | in the repository's base dir |
324	| planner run | `crustify/planner/run-<n>` | in the repository's base dir, while its run is live |
325	| module | `crustify/modules/<link-unit>/<module>`, or `crustify/foundational/<link-unit>/<module>` for a foundational module | in its worktree, while it integrates |
326	| wave | `crustify/waves/wave-<index>` | never |
327	| batch | `crustify/batches/wave-<index>/batch-<index>` | in its worktree |
328	
329	The shipping branch holds what the user has approved to ship: it advances only with the
330	user's approval, by a fast-forward to the working branch, and each advance is tagged on it,
331	`ship-<n>` numbered from 1, or `crustify/ship-<n>` in an audit. The working branch is where the
332	campaign integrates its work: planner runs fork from it and are promoted back to it, and
333	the modules are integrated into it, as `scheduling` describes.
334	
335	A module's branch holds one run of its waves: its waves fork from
336	it and are promoted back to it, and it is integrated into the working branch once they
337	have landed, as [Integration](#45-integration) describes. `<module>` is the module's
338	`name`, the path of its TU or header below the C root; a path is never a directory of
339	another, so no two module branches collide.
340	
341	A wave's branch is the integration branch its batches land on, a review wave's as much as
342	a translation wave's. It is never checked out: a landing push to a checked-out branch
343	fails, and one to a missing branch silently creates it.
344	
345	An audit has no link units or modules: its waves are review waves, laid out the same
346	way.
347	
348	## 3. Worktrees
349	
350	Each batch has its own worktree, its `c/` a worktree of the base checkout's submodule, at
351	`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/<batch id>`, named as
352	[`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s Ids section names them, so that its name tells which
353	module it works on, and so does a module while it integrates, at
354	`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/integration`, beside its batches'. A
355	planner run has none: it runs in the repository's base dir, on its branch.
356	
357	## 4. Landing
358	
359	A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
360	out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
361	no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
362	subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
363	objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
364	and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
365	`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
366	and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
367	progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
368	repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
369	[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.
370	
371	The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
372	the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
373	update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
374	enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.
375	
376	### 4.1 The landing lock
377	
378	An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
379	exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
380	`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:
381	
382	```text
383	$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
384	```
385	
386	A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
387	until its landing has succeeded:
388	
389	1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
390	2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
391	   lands while it holds the lock;
392	3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
393	   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
394	   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
395	4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
396	5. it releases the lock.
397	
398	A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
399	that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.
400	
401	The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
402	and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
403	its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
404	CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
405	that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
406	holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
407	and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
408	and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
409	walking up the shell's parent processes:
410	<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
411	documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->
412	
413	```bash
414	lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
415	mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
416	# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
417	sh -c '
418	  exec 9>"$1"
419	  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
420	  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
421	' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
422	# release, once the push has succeeded
423	holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
424	```
425	
426	The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
427	that a release never removes the next holder's record.
428	
429	The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
430	stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
431	agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
432	running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
433	record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.
434	
435	### 4.2 Commits
436	
437	Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
438	commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
439	base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
440	neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
441	become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.
442	
443	The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
444	pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
445	describes.
446	<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
447	remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
448	it. -->
449	
450	### 4.3 Promotion
451	
452	A wave that has landed every batch is promoted to the branch it forked from, the module's
453	branch or the working branch, by a fast-forward to its tip, with the same local push
454	through the Git common directory, which rejects anything but a fast-forward.
455	
456	### 4.4 Progress
457	
458	The progress recorded while waves run, in `schedule.json`, the dashboard's usage and
459	campaign cells, and the `status` of a module in `modules.json` that a wrap batch ahead of
460	its consumer freezes, is committed on the working branch whenever no module is integrating. No agent writes
461	`schedule.json`, and no module branch changes it.
462	
463	### 4.5 Integration
464	
465	A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
466	last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
467	it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
468	other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
469	record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.
470	
471	1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
472	   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
473	   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
474	   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
475	   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
476	   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
477	   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
478	   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
479	   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
480	2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
481	   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
482	   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
483	   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
484	   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
485	   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
486	   over are listed before its C tests leave.
487	3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.
488	
489	Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
490	one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
491	their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
492	the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.
493	
494	## 5. Lifecycle
495	
496	Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
497	only it needed is purged.
498	
499	### 5.1 Campaign
500	
501	The working branch is created during setup, in the repository the campaign creates, with
502	the C under `c/` and `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` in its first commit. The shipping branch is created at the same commit and stays there
503	until the user first approves shipping. Both last for the campaign.
504	
505	The working branch is committed to only when nothing is being promoted or integrated to
506	it, so that every promotion and integration is a fast-forward: the progress recorded in
507	the meantime stays in the base checkout's working tree until then, as
508	[Progress](#44-progress) describes.
509	
510	### 5.2 Planner runs
511	
512	A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
513	branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.
514	
515	### 5.3 Modules
516	
517	A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and
518	the settings it runs under, committed before its first wave.
519	
520	A module's branch is forked from its base before its first wave,
521	once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
522	whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
523	consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
524	[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
525	from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
526	module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
527	its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
528	are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.
529	
530	### 5.4 Waves
531	
532	A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
533	later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
534	before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
535	requires; that commit is the wave's base.
536	Once every batch has landed, the wave is promoted, as [Promotion](#43-promotion)
537	describes, and its branch purged.
538	
539	A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
540	they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.
541	
542	### 5.5 Batches
543	
544	A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
545	launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
546	not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
547	and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
548	records, since no batch changes the C.
549	Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
550	recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
551	[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
552	inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.
553	
554	## 6. Identity
555	
556	Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
557	as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
558	`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
559	unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
560	as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
561	message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
562	agent's host suggests included.
563	
564	The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
565	that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
566	host may have no git identity of its own.
567

---
name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, the record of what landed and how evolution itself evolves. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as
its `PROPOSAL.md`: the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it
cites; its destination; the change, or the patch; how it was validated; its review's
verdict; and its status, `open`, `landed`, with the commit it landed as, or `declined`,
with why. A lesson is not
filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it.

A defect in a tool found while reviewing is such a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed
code, and is filed with its reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each is one rule, with the evidence it rests on and its scope, the
modules, items or stages it holds for. A lesson a second campaign records again is
generalized into the spec, by a proposal citing both.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [Record](#11-record) describes.

## 8. Review

Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
one that made it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks
that:

- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;
- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;
- it is placed and written as [`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md) describes, and states
  no rule in the target's names;
- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
- its entry of [Record](#11-record), which the change or its proposal drafts, names a
  recurrence signal a campaign would observe, and `test` only where its test checks all of
  it; and
- whether it weakens a check, which the verdict marks.

A review runs under the campaign's working branch of the component, never under the change
it reviews, and reads the change from its branch. Its task pins the commit it reviews, and
only that commit lands, by a fast-forward of the working branch: a commit added after the
verdict, or one a rebase or cherry-pick makes, is reviewed again. Its checks are this section's and its
role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided, a status of [Record](#11-record) a check changes or a
proposal's status, verdict and review, changes no rule and is not reviewed; an entry is
reviewed with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it,
without the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else
runs on it. `GOALS.md` is the exception: a change to it is proposed, never made, since it
is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: recurring lessons are
proposed for the spec, open proposals are landed as the autonomy allows, the working
branches are offered to the user for `devel`, the revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled, and the watched changes
of the record are checked against the module, as an audit checks them at its end.

## 11. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. An entry gives the campaign and proposal the change
came from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence
signal and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change
no proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came
from. The entry is drafted with its change, in the change itself for a
change to Crustify and in its proposal for a change to a tool, so that the review reads it,
and is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign as the change lands. The record holds every
change landed since it began, on 2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is checked at each module's end, and at an audit's end, in every campaign,
against that module's or audit's findings, failed runs, proposals and corrections. It is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the entry: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that
  passed it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign, each entry with its
change and each check at its module's end, and reaches `devel` with it. Rows are appended
in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge of two campaigns' working
branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the check still runs and its statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, it does not run.

## 12. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [Signals](#2-signals) lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

name: versioning
description: "Repositories, branches, worktrees, landing under the landing lock, promotion, integration, their lifecycle, and the identity every commit takes. Read before the first commit, and before creating, landing on, promoting or purging any branch or worktree."
---

# Versioning

How a campaign's work is held in version control: the repositories it works in, their
branches and worktrees, how a batch lands its work and how each part is promoted. Where
things sit in the tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Repositories

A translation campaign produces a Rust codebase, so its repository is one: a new
repository created for the campaign, with the Rust at its root and the C it translates
inside it.

| campaign | repository | the C, under `c/` |
|---|---|---|
| wrap | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the source, pinned at the campaign's revision, which the campaign never changes |
| port | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the campaign's fork of the source, `<repo>-fork`, on its `main` branch, which the modules' switches trim as they leave C |

`<repo>` is the source repository's name: a campaign on libgit2 is `libgit2-crustify`,
and a port's fork `libgit2-fork`. A wrap and a port campaign share the name, since wrapping a
codebase is a step towards replacing its implementation: a port continues a wrap campaign
in its repository. Both keep the C's history where it belongs, so that it can be read in the
submodule and an upstream release taken in by rebasing the fork's `main` onto it. The fork
mirrors the source's own `main` as `upstream/main`. The repositories are created under the
`crustify-rs` organization; the campaign's tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

A library the target uses from outside its tree is wrapped in a wrap campaign of its own,
in `<source>-crustify`, named after the source it is built from, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md) describes.

An audit reviews an existing Rust crate in its own repository, and creates none.

## 2. Branches

| branch | name | checked out |
|---|---|---|
| shipping | `main` in the campaign's own repository; `crustify/main` in an audit, beside the reviewed crate's own branches | never while the campaign runs |
| working | `crustify/devel` | in the repository's base dir |
| planner run | `crustify/planner/run-<n>` | in the repository's base dir, while its run is live |
| module | `crustify/modules/<link-unit>/<module>`, or `crustify/foundational/<link-unit>/<module>` for a foundational module | in its worktree, while it integrates |
| wave | `crustify/waves/wave-<index>` | never |
| batch | `crustify/batches/wave-<index>/batch-<index>` | in its worktree |

The shipping branch holds what the user has approved to ship: it advances only with the
user's approval, by a fast-forward to the working branch, and each advance is tagged on it,
`ship-<n>` numbered from 1, or `crustify/ship-<n>` in an audit. The working branch is where the
campaign integrates its work: planner runs fork from it and are promoted back to it, and
the modules are integrated into it, as `scheduling` describes.

A module's branch holds one run of its waves: its waves fork from
it and are promoted back to it, and it is integrated into the working branch once they
have landed, as [Integration](#45-integration) describes. `<module>` is the module's
`name`, the path of its TU or header below the C root; a path is never a directory of
another, so no two module branches collide.

A wave's branch is the integration branch its batches land on, a review wave's as much as
a translation wave's. It is never checked out: a landing push to a checked-out branch
fails, and one to a missing branch silently creates it.

An audit has no link units or modules: its waves are review waves, laid out the same
way.

## 3. Worktrees

Each batch has its own worktree, its `c/` a worktree of the base checkout's submodule, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/<batch id>`, named as
[`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s Ids section names them, so that its name tells which
module it works on, and so does a module while it integrates, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/integration`, beside its batches'. A
planner run has none: it runs in the repository's base dir, on its branch.

## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

A wave that has landed every batch is promoted to the branch it forked from, the module's
branch or the working branch, by a fast-forward to its tip, with the same local push
through the Git common directory, which rejects anything but a fast-forward.

### 4.4 Progress

The progress recorded while waves run, in `schedule.json`, the dashboard's usage and
campaign cells, and the `status` of a module in `modules.json` that a wrap batch ahead of
its consumer freezes, is committed on the working branch whenever no module is integrating. No agent writes
`schedule.json`, and no module branch changes it.

### 4.5 Integration

A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.

1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
   over are listed before its C tests leave.
3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.

Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.

## 5. Lifecycle

Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
only it needed is purged.

### 5.1 Campaign

The working branch is created during setup, in the repository the campaign creates, with
the C under `c/` and `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` in its first commit. The shipping branch is created at the same commit and stays there
until the user first approves shipping. Both last for the campaign.

The working branch is committed to only when nothing is being promoted or integrated to
it, so that every promotion and integration is a fast-forward: the progress recorded in
the meantime stays in the base checkout's working tree until then, as
[Progress](#44-progress) describes.

### 5.2 Planner runs

A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.

### 5.3 Modules

A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and
the settings it runs under, committed before its first wave.

A module's branch is forked from its base before its first wave,
once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.

### 5.4 Waves

A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
requires; that commit is the wave's base.
Once every batch has landed, the wave is promoted, as [Promotion](#43-promotion)
describes, and its branch purged.

A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
records, since no batch changes the C.
Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.

name: accounting
description: "The dashboard, its cells, the runs' records and transcripts, and how cost and time are derived. Read before filling dashboard cells or collecting a run's records."
---

# Accounting

What a campaign records about its own work: the dashboard, the runs' records and
transcripts its figures come from, and how cost and time are derived from them.

## 1. The dashboard

The dashboard, `crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md` unless the settings name another, is the
campaign's record of what each planner run, batch, wave and module did and cost. It is
filled from `templates/translate/dashboard.template.md`, an audit's from
`templates/audit/dashboard.template.md`, and keeps the template's format exactly.
When an adopted Crustify change adds a table or a column to the template, it is
added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
